questions.q: What is matching, as defined in this lesson?
options: Backing up records to a secondary database
Comparing records, within one system or across several, to decide whether they represent the same real-world entity
Deleting duplicate records automatically without review
Encrypting sensitive fields before storage
questions.explain: Matching is the comparison process that decides whether two records refer to the same real-world thing — the mechanical heart of MDM.

questions.q: What does this lesson say the output of a match process usually looks like?
options: Always a simple, binary yes or no with no middle ground
A spectrum: confidently the same, confidently different, or uncertain enough to need a human
A random number with no business meaning
Always 'uncertain,' since matching can never be confident
questions.explain: The lesson explicitly describes the output as a spectrum rather than pure binary, setting up Lesson 7's deterministic/probabilistic distinction and Lesson 11's steward review.

questions.q: Which of these is given as an example of a match key?
options: The server's IP address
A unique identifier such as a tax ID, or name plus address when no reliable ID exists
The file format the record is stored in
The time zone of the database server
questions.explain: Match keys are the fields actually compared — the lesson lists unique identifiers, name plus address, email, and weighted composites as examples.

options: It prevents unauthorized users from accessing the database
It avoids comparing every record to every other record, which doesn't scale, by grouping records into smaller sets first using a coarse attribute
It automatically fixes typos in customer names
It encrypts match keys for security
questions.explain: Blocking groups records by a cheap, coarse attribute like zip code so detailed matching only runs within each block, avoiding an impractical 'everyone vs. everyone' comparison.

questions.q: Per this lesson, why is name plus address a common but imperfect match key?
options: Because it is illegal to use in most countries
Because it is sensitive to typos, nicknames, and formatting differences like 'St.' vs. 'Street'
Because addresses never change
Because names are always unique across an entire population
questions.explain: The lesson notes name plus address is the common fallback when no reliable unique ID exists, but flags its sensitivity to minor variations in how the same facts get written down.
